Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "hey, can you help me make a family dinner calendar for two weeks, monday october 5 through sunday october 18, 2026. this is for our household, not a general meal plan: me, elena, my husband marco, nina who is eleven, and leo who is seven. we only need dinners on it, not breakfasts or lunches. please give every date in that range its own line so i can see the whole stretch, including weekends, rather than just a list of meal ideas. normally we try to eat around 6:30, though some evenings need a little thought because of the kids' activities and marco's work hours.

ruth, marco's mother, is coming for dinner on thursday october 8 and thursday october 15, so please show five servings on those two dates and four servings on all the other dates. she has a peanut allergy, and on the two nights she is here the meal should contain no peanut ingredients. nina won't eat mushrooms, and leo finds hot spice too strong; mild seasoning is fine. those are the food details we know, and i'd like the calendar to use them without turning it into a special separate plate for every person. we are not asking for medical or nutrition advice, just dinner suggestions that fit those preferences and the visit dates.

wednesdays are swim nights. the children get home around 6:20, so dinner on october 7 and 14 can be served at 6:45 instead of the usual 6:30. something that can be reheated or finished quickly after we get back would help on those two dates. marco told me, “Tuesday is the only night I can cook before 7.” please keep that timing in mind when you assign a cook or describe prep. don't assume he can cook before 7 on other days; i haven't given you anyone else's detailed work schedule, so don't make one up. there isn't a special serving-time change for any other date.

on school nights, monday through friday, we prefer no more than 30 minutes of active prep. that doesn't have to mean the food is finished in 30 minutes if it can cook on its own. saturday can be more relaxed. on sundays, a make-ahead step of up to 45 minutes is okay if you say what the step is and which later dinner it helps with, but it's optional. we usually like to have leftovers on friday, so leave friday october 9 and friday october 16 as leftover dinners rather than giving us a new recipe for those nights. if the information here doesn't support a particular detail, just leave that detail open instead of guessing.

here is what we already have and you may use the pantry inventory pasted here when suggesting meals: two cups of rice, two cans of chickpeas, one box of pasta, one jar of tomato sauce, a bag of frozen peas, eight tortillas, a block of cheddar, and six eggs. i have not checked the quantities of anything else in the kitchen, so don't treat unlisted ingredients as things we definitely have. please give a separate shopping list for ingredients the suggested dinners need beyond this inventory. group that list by produce, refrigerated items, and pantry or other items; if a quantity depends on a recipe or serving size we haven't specified, flag it rather than making up an exact amount. the list should be usable for shopping for the dates in this calendar, not a running list for other weeks.

for the actual calendar, a plain text table would be easiest for me to print. use columns for date and day, dinner, servings, and a brief prep or timing note. keep the meal description short, not a full recipe. include who is cooking only where the details i gave make that clear, especially around tuesday; otherwise don't assign a person. for wednesday, show the 6:45 time and the quick-finish or reheating point. the two thursday visits should be easy to spot, and the friday leftover nights should be labeled as leftovers. do not open cloud links. i am pasting the relevant information here, and you may use it to make the calendar and shopping list.

one last practical thing, this will go on the fridge where the kids can read it, so keep the date labels and wording straightforward and make the final output plain text rather than relying on a spreadsheet. after the calendar and shopping list, don't add a separate meal-prep essay; the optional sunday prep note can sit with the sunday entry it relates to. if you mention a make-ahead step, identify its later dinner plainly so it doesn't get confused with that day's meal.", "output": "Create a two-week family dinner calendar for Monday, October 5 through Sunday, October 18, 2026, with a separate entry for every date, including weekends. Include dinners only, not breakfasts or lunches. The household is Elena, her husband Marco, their eleven-year-old Nina, and seven-year-old Leo.

1. Dates, servings, and food preferences

Ruth, Marco’s mother, will join dinner on Thursday, October 8, and Thursday, October 15. Show five servings on those dates and four servings on every other date. Ruth has a peanut allergy, so dinners on her two visit dates must contain no peanut ingredients. Nina will not eat mushrooms, and Leo finds hot spice too strong; mild seasoning is fine. Suggest meals that fit these preferences without planning a separate plate for each person. No medical or nutrition advice is needed.

2. Timing and preparation

The usual dinner time is around 6:30. On Wednesday, October 7, and Wednesday, October 14, the children get home from swim at around 6:20, so dinner may be served at 6:45 instead. For those two dinners, suggest something that can be reheated or finished quickly after they return.

Marco said, “Tuesday is the only night I can cook before 7.” Keep that timing in mind when assigning a cook or describing preparation. Do not assume he can cook before 7 on other days. No detailed work schedule has been provided for anyone else, so do not assign them one. No other date has a special serving-time change.

From Monday through Friday, limit active preparation to 30 minutes. The food may take longer overall if it can cook unattended. Saturday can be more relaxed. On Sundays, an optional make-ahead step of up to 45 minutes is acceptable. If you include one, state what it is and which later dinner it helps with. Leave unsupported details open rather than guessing.

Keep Friday, October 9, and Friday, October 16, as leftover dinners; do not suggest new recipes for those dates.

3. Available ingredients and shopping list

You may use this pantry inventory: two cups of rice, two cans of chickpeas, one box of pasta, one jar of tomato sauce, a bag of frozen peas, eight tortillas, a block of cheddar, and six eggs. Other kitchen quantities have not been checked, so do not assume unlisted ingredients are already available.

After the calendar, provide a separate shopping list for ingredients the suggested dinners need beyond the inventory. Group items under produce, refrigerated items, and pantry or other items. If a quantity depends on a recipe or serving size that has not been specified, flag it rather than inventing an exact amount. The list should cover only these calendar dates.

4. Output format

Use a plain-text table that is easy to print, with columns for date and day, dinner, servings, and a brief preparation or timing note. Keep meal descriptions short rather than giving full recipes. Assign a cook only where the information provided makes that clear, especially around Tuesday; otherwise leave the cook unassigned. Show the 6:45 dinner time and the reheating or quick-finish detail for both Wednesdays. Make Ruth’s Thursday visits and the Friday leftover dinners easy to identify. Do not open cloud links; use the information provided here to make the calendar and shopping list.

Keep the date labels and wording straightforward for children reading the calendar on the fridge. Do not rely on a spreadsheet or add a separate meal-preparation essay after the calendar and shopping list. If you include an optional Sunday make-ahead step, place it with that Sunday’s entry and clearly identify the later dinner it supports."}]
